questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted a destination where I could combine clinical training with language immersion. Gijón offered the opportunity to gain hands-on experience in a hospital setting while improving my Spanish skills. Additionally, the chance to experience a different healthcare system and live in a culturally rich and naturally beautiful region like Asturias made Universidad de Oviedo an ideal choice. Furthermore, since I did not have more SU, the Erasmus grant was crucial.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very little information was provided in advance by the international office or faculty coordinator. Fortunately, the local Erasmus Student Network (ESN) offered support. Practical details—such as hospital schedules, a hospital map, and course expectations—only became clear on my first day at the hospital. I also had to change the order of my rotations due to coordination issues between departments. However, once I found the right administrative office, things started falling into place. What I learned most from my stay in Spain was this: everything will eventually work out—it just requires more patience, flexibility, and acceptance of limited upfront information.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found our apartment through Idealista. It took some time to find a nice place, but we eventually ended up with an amazing apartment in the La Arena neighborhood—right on the beachfront. If your budget allows, I highly recommend looking for something similar. Living by the beach made the experience even more special and was a great way to enjoy Gijón outside of hospital hours.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Most students live off campus in Gijón, as there are limited student housing options. Rent is generally affordable compared to other European cities, but it can take time to find the right place—especially if you're looking for short-term leases. Be prepared to communicate in Spanish with landlords, and always ask for photos, videos, or even a virtual tour before committing.

Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration process was somewhat unclear at first. I was told I had to wait until December to register for February rotations, which made obtaining pre-approval and completing my grant applications difficult. However, with persistence and many phone calls, I managed to outline a plan for the rotations I wanted. Although the schedule was later adjusted, I ultimately secured all my preferred placements.

I did not receive much information in advance, so I had to be proactive upon arrival. I visited the international office at Hospital de Cabueñes and met the coordinator in person to arrange my clinical rotations. Some departments were not well coordinated, requiring me to adjust the order of my rotations initially. Once I identified the correct contacts, the process became much smoother. Flexibility and patience were essential throughout.

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
All of my time was spent on rotations rather than traditional lectures, so the “course level” was like clinical rotations in Denmark. Because all instruction and patient interactions were in Spanish, I not only practiced terminology and patient–doctor communication but also had to think and respond quickly in a second language, which added an extra layer of challenge and learning.

Compared to Denmark, I found that specialists in each department had more time to teach and mentor students. In some rotations, I could spend a full hour discussing a complex case with a consultant or observing a procedure step-by-step—opportunities that are rarer back home due to faster patient turnover. The work culture was different, too: doctors often worked longer hours overall but took regular, relaxed breaks. It wasn’t unusual for a consultant to pause mid‐morning for a coffee and a chat about teaching points, research interests, or cultural differences in patient care. That unhurried atmosphere made it easier to ask questions, refine clinical skills, and absorb new practices, all while refining my Spanish in a supportive environment.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Adjusting to the local culture in Gijón was relatively easy, especially with an open mind and a bit of patience. People were warm, welcoming, and curious about international students. The pace of life was slower than in Denmark, and I had to get used to the later meal times and more flexible approach to time and organization. Once I embraced that, I really enjoyed the relaxed atmosphere, social coffee breaks, and strong sense of community.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: One of the most challenging cultural differences was the lack of structure and punctuality compared to what I’m used to in Denmark. Information was often provided at the last minute, and schedules could change without much notice. It required flexibility and sometimes a bit of persistence to get things organized. Also, the late meal times and long lunch breaks took some getting used to, but over time I adapted and came to appreciate the more relaxed rhythm of daily life.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I especially appreciated the warmth and openness of the people in Gijón. There was a strong sense of community, and I often experienced genuine interest and kindness from both hospital staff and locals. I also enjoyed the relaxed pace of life, the daily social rituals like coffee breaks, and the emphasis on enjoying good food and conversation. The natural beauty of Asturias—with its beaches, mountains, and green landscapes—added to the overall experience and made everyday life feel rich and balanced.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be flexible and proactive – The organization can be less structured than at UCPH. You might not get all the information you need in advance, so be ready to ask questions, show up in person, and follow up multiple times if necessary. Things usually work out—but not always on the first try.
Learn as much Spanish as you can beforehand – Most communication at the hospital (and in daily life) is in Spanish. Having a solid foundation in the language will make both your clinical learning and social experience much smoother and more rewarding.
Enjoy the local culture – Embrace the slower pace, take part in social rituals like coffee breaks, and explore Asturias’ stunning nature. Living in Gijón offers a great balance between professional growth and personal enjoyment—make the most of both!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Yes—here’s a final tip that could be useful for future exchange students:

Bring more patience than you think you’ll need. The administrative processes can feel unstructured, and communication is often last-minute. Don’t panic—ask around, visit offices in person, and talk to other students or hospital staff. Things will eventually fall into place.

Also, consider arriving a bit early to settle in, get to know the city, and practice your Spanish. And if possible, live close to the city center—walking along the beach is a luxury that makes every day better!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was gaining the confidence to communicate effectively in Spanish in a clinical setting. Being able to take patient histories, discuss treatment plans with doctors, and truly connect across language and cultural barriers was incredibly fulfilling. It also gave me a new perspective on healthcare and deepened my understanding of what it means to be a good, empathetic doctor—no matter where in the world you are.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge during the exchange was the lack of structure and clear communication, especially in the beginning. Information about rotations, schedules, and expectations was limited or provided at the last minute, which made planning difficult. I had to be very proactive, flexible, and persistent to get the information I needed and ensure that everything worked out. While it was frustrating at times, it also taught me valuable lessons in adaptability and problem-solving.
